title: Friday, August 28, 2026

headline.title: Yesterday's semi bid unwound completely, and it took one overnight print to do it. MRVL fell 10.29% to 216.62 after reporting, and the read-through ran straight through the complex: SMH −3.47% the session after it closed at its own high, NVDA −4.57% giving back half of Thursday's +8.74%, AMD −2.32%, DELL −3.39%. XLK −1.55% after +3.16% the day before. The two sectors that carried Thursday were the two worst on Friday.
headline.summary: And the rotation went the other way rather than simply selling off. Five of twelve sectors closed green — XLC +1.42%, XLY +1.15%, XLE +0.63%, XLP +0.43%, XLF +0.38% — while tech and semis took the damage. SPY held at −0.23% and QQQ at −0.65%, but IWM −1.35% was the weakest of the three. All of it around Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote as Chair at 9:00am CT, with July core PCE ahead of it — the first policy framing from a new Chair rather than a restatement of a known one. PYPL fell 12.71% on its own news, the Advent/Stripe approach at $60.50 a share rejected.

what_happened: One earnings print reversed an entire sector in a session.

MRVL had faded its whole gap into Thursday's close, reported that night, and opened 225.255 against a 241.45 close. It made its high at 228.88 in the opening minutes and closed 216.62, near a 215.55 low, −10.29% on 49.0M shares. The read-through was immediate and complete: SMH went from +3.10% Thursday to −3.47% Friday, and NVDA from +8.74% to −4.57%. Thursday's two green sectors were Friday's two worst.
NVDA failed at 230 for the second consecutive session.

Thursday it ran to 230.47 and closed 227.98, back below. Friday it opened 227.36, reached only 229.26, and then lost 12.45 points to a 216.81 low before closing 217.55. Two sessions, two rejections at the same round number, and the second one gave back more than half the beat-and-raise move. The morning note had it precisely: “tagged 230 and failed”, with premarket at 227.02 already back inside.
It was a rotation, not a liquidation.

Five sectors closed green while tech and semis were sold: XLC +1.42%, XLY +1.15%, XLE +0.63%, XLP +0.43%, XLF +0.38%. SPY only lost 0.23% because the money that left semis largely stayed in the market. The exception was small caps — IWM −1.35%, the weakest index — which is the piece that looks like genuine de-risking into a Fed unknown rather than a sector switch.

how_played_out: The three ranked calls were all correct and all three were shorts or defensives.

MRVL −10.29% on a failed 2U that was visible the previous afternoon, PYPL −12.71% on a removed deal premium where the chart already agreed with the news, and AAPL +1.63% on an inside day resolving up in the lowest-implied-move name on the sheet. Three for three, and the common thread is that none of them required predicting the Jackson Hole reaction — each had a structure that was already resolved or nearly so before Warsh spoke.
A single overnight print reversed an entire sector, and Thursday's tape had already warned about it.

MRVL gave back its whole gap on Thursday, closing 241.45 near the low after opening 253.44 — and that was before it reported. The morning note on Thursday had flagged it as an inside day gapping out into an event, and the fade into the close was the market pricing the risk in advance. Friday then delivered −10.29%, and the read-through took SMH from +3.10% to −3.47% and NVDA from +8.74% to −4.57%. Thursday's two green sectors were Friday's two worst, in that order.
NVDA failing twice at the same number is worth more than either failure alone.

Thursday's high was 230.47, Friday's was 229.26, and both sessions closed well below. One rejection at a round number is noise; two consecutive ones with a 12.45-point reversal on the second define a level. The morning note wrote “tagged 230 and failed” with premarket already back inside at 227.02 — the call was not a prediction so much as a refusal to treat Thursday's beat-and-raise as unfinished business.
The rotation held the index up and the small caps gave it away.

Five sectors green — XLC +1.42%, XLY +1.15%, XLE, XLP, XLF — kept SPY to −0.23% while tech and semis were sold hard. That is money moving rather than leaving. The one piece that does not fit the rotation story is IWM −1.35%, materially worse than either large-cap index, which reads as genuine de-risking ahead of an unknown from a new Fed Chair. Watching the two together separated a sector switch from a market-wide reduction.

lessons: A name that fades its gap into its own print has already told you the answer.

MRVL opened 253.44 on Thursday and closed 241.45 near the low, before reporting. That giveback was the market pricing the event, and Friday's −10.29% only confirmed it. The tradeable observation is not the earnings reaction — it is the session before it, where a gap that cannot hold into a known catalyst is the market declining to underwrite the outcome.
Two consecutive rejections at the same level define it; one does not.

NVDA reached 230.47 Thursday and 229.26 Friday, closing far below both times, with a 12.45-point reversal on the second attempt. After Thursday alone the tag looked like an extension of a beat-and-raise; after Friday it is a ceiling. Waiting for the second test cost the first move and bought a level that can actually be traded against.
A sector that closes at its high is not safer the next morning — sometimes it is the opposite.

SMH closed 573.00 against a 573.21 high on Thursday, the strongest possible finish, and opened the next session into a −3.47% day on a single overnight print from a component. A close at the high says the day ended with buyers in control; it says nothing about what lands overnight, and this stretch has repeatedly shown that the overnight gap carries more of the move than the prior candle does.
Green sectors on a red tech day tell you whether it is rotation or exit — and IWM tells you if that read is wrong.

Five sectors green kept SPY to −0.23% while semis fell 3.47%, which reads cleanly as rotation. But IWM −1.35% did not participate in any of it. Small caps underperforming both large-cap indices while five sectors rise is the tell that some of the money was leaving rather than moving, and checking those two facts against each other is a better read on a Fed day than either one alone.
tomorrow: Monday is month-end. Rebalancing into the close carries no direction, and the late-session volume spike should not be read as information. MSCI adds SNDK, CRS and ATI to the World Index at the close — mechanical buying on a fixed date.

Closed 53.66, −12.71%, with the $60.50/share Advent/Stripe premium out of the price on 36.3M shares. Deal premiums do not re-enter on their own; the question is where a standalone valuation sits, not whether the approach returns.

Carry into next week: the index barely moved while its leadership completely inverted in one session. Thursday's two green sectors were Friday's two worst, and small caps underperformed through both. If the same two sectors can flip the whole tape on a single component's earnings, the concentration is the risk — not the direction.

tts.label: Lessons
tts.text: Four things to carry forward. First, a name that fades its gap into its own print has already told you the answer. Marvell opened two fifty three forty four Thursday and closed two forty one forty five near the low, before reporting. That giveback was the market pricing the event, and Friday only confirmed it. Second, two consecutive rejections at the same level define it and one does not. Nvidia reached two thirty forty seven Thursday and two twenty nine twenty six Friday, closing far below both times. After Thursday it looked like an extension. After Friday it is a ceiling. Third, a sector that closes at its high is not safer the next morning, and sometimes it is the opposite. Semis closed twenty one cents off their high Thursday and opened into a three and a half percent decline on one overnight print from a component. Fourth, green sectors on a red tech day tell you whether it is rotation or exit, and small caps tell you if that read is wrong. Five sectors rose while semis fell three and a half percent, which reads as rotation, but small caps underperformed both large cap indices, which reads as de risking.
